title: The Impact of Online Games on Creativity and the Role of Imagination
author: Cheng, Yung-hsun
summary: Research from Taiwan finds young people highly motivated to play online games display higher imagination and measurable creativity, with imagination mediating the games-creativity link. The findings complicate flat moral narratives about screens, showing that not all digital engagement is equivalent. Active construction in sandbox games and immersion in narrative worlds appears to work on the mind differently than passive scrolling. The posture of the self matters more than the medium.
points: Young people motivated to play online games show higher imagination and measurable creativity; imagination mediates the games-creativity relationship.
Not all screen time is equivalent; active construction differs fundamentally from passive consumption in psychological effects.
Sandbox games like Roblox and narrative-rich worlds like Genshin Impact work on the mind differently than passive scrolling platforms.
The posture of the self—engaged agency versus dulled consumption—matters more than the medium itself.
Active construction and imaginative engagement through gaming can support creativity, contradicting blanket screen-time restrictions.
quotes: Young people who are highly motivated to play online games tend to display higher imagination, and imagination in turn supports measurable creativity.
Active construction in sandbox games like Roblox, and immersion in narrative-rich worlds like Genshin Impact, appears to work on the mind differently than passive scrolling.
The posture of the self matters more than the medium, and that engaged agency is spiritually different from dulled consumption.
Games are not thereby harmless. The study's actual point is that the posture of the self matters more than the medium.” Archived from Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
